pageInfo.subtitle: Master the art of landing on strong chord tones, guide tones, and melodic destinations using chromatic approaches and enclosures.
pageInfo.heroDescription: The defining hallmark of master improvisers—from Charlie Parker and Joe Pass to Larry Carlton and Grant Green—is intentionality. Rather than noodling blindly through scale patterns, elite soloists target specific harmonic destinations before they even pick the first note. In this masterclass, you will learn to navigate chord progressions by targeting 3rds and 7ths on strong beats, voice-lead smoothly across changes, and embellish your landings with chromatic approaches and bebop enclosures.

guidelines.title: The Architecture of Target Note Soloing

items.text: Downbeat Harmonic Gravity: Landing strong chord tones (especially the 3rd or Root) squarely on beats 1 and 3 instantly locks your solo into the rhythm section.
The Magnetic 3rd & 7th: Guide tones dictate whether a chord is major, minor, or dominant; targeting them outlines the harmony without needing backing chords.
Chromatic Approaches: Leading into your destination from a half-step below or above generates irresistible forward momentum and release.
Bebop Enclosures: Surrounding a target pitch from above (diatonic) and below (chromatic) creates sophisticated, authentic jazz phrasing.
Rhythmic Anticipation: Striking your target note on the 'and' of beat 4 before the bar line pulls the listener forward into the coming chord change.
Reverse Phrase Construction: Choose your landing note and beat first, then work backward to construct the scale or chromatic line leading up to it.
CAGED Shape Visualization: Anchor every target note inside a familiar chord grip so you instantly recognize its harmonic function (1, 3, 5, or 7).
Minimal Motion Voice Leading: Connect chord changes by identifying target notes that move by just a half-step or whole-step between adjacent chords.
Tension-Release Dynamics: Spend weak subdivisions on dissonant scale steps or chromatic passing tones so the target arrival feels profoundly satisfying.
Vocal Articulation: Use slides, slurs, and vibrato on target notes to emphasize arrival rather than treating every note with identical mechanical attack.

exercises.title: Downbeat Landing: Targeting 3rds Over ii-V-I
exercises.description: The 3rd of each chord carries its fundamental emotional quality. In this 4-measure ii-V-I study in C major, practice landing squarely on the 3rd of each chord on beat 1: F on Dm7, B on G7, and E on Cmaj7. Notice how each chord change is immediately obvious to the listener even without a backing track.

patternNote.text: Targets on Beat 1: F (b3 of Dm7, fret 6 string 2) ➔ B (3rd of G7, fret 4 string 3) ➔ E (3rd of Cmaj7, fret 5 string 2)

notation.title: Targeting 3rds Across ii-V-I
notation.staveTitle: Targeting the 3rd on Beat 1 of Each Measure

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: Play along with a metronome at 76 BPM. Emphasize beat 1 with a confident pick stroke and subtle vibrato, letting the target 3rd ring clearly over the change.

exercises.title: Guide Tone Voice Leading (7th Resolving to 3rd)
exercises.description: In jazz, blues, and neo-soul harmony, the most potent voice leading occurs when the 7th of one chord resolves down by half-step to the 3rd of the next chord. Here, the 7th of Dm7 (C, fret 5 string 3) steps down a half-step to the 3rd of G7 (B, fret 4 string 3), and the 7th of G7 (F, fret 6 string 2) steps down to the 3rd of Cmaj7 (E, fret 5 string 2).

patternNote.text: Smooth Half-Step Connection: Dm7 (7th: C) ➔ G7 (3rd: B) | G7 (7th: F) ➔ Cmaj7 (3rd: E)

notation.title: 7th to 3rd Guide Tone Voice Leading
notation.staveTitle: Tracing the 7th ➔ 3rd Half-Step Voice Leading Path

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: Observe how smoothly the melody glides across the chord changes. Guide tone lines are the foundation of fluent bebop and modern guitar soloing.

exercises.title: Chromatic Approach From Below
exercises.description: Leading into your target note from a half-step below creates tension that releases immediately when you strike the target pitch on beat 1. In this study over Am - Dm - G - C, each measure ends with a chromatic pickup note that slides up one fret into the new chord's target note.

patternNote.text: Pickup Formula: Play 1 half-step below on the 'and' of 4 ➔ slide into the target chord tone on beat 1

notation.title: Chromatic Approach From Below
notation.staveTitle: Half-Step Chromatic Pickup into Strong Beat Targets

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: Focus on the transition between bars. The chromatic note on the last eighth note should sound intentional, leaning into the target downbeat with momentum.

exercises.title: Bebop Chromatic Enclosures (Above & Below)
exercises.description: An enclosure frames your target note like a bullseye: you play one diatonic scale step above, followed by one chromatic half-step below, before finally resolving squarely onto your target note on the downbeat. This exercise applies enclosures to targets across Dm7, G7, and Cmaj7.

patternNote.text: Enclosure Anatomy: Diatonic Above ➔ Chromatic Below ➔ Target Note Resolution

notation.title: Bebop Chromatic Enclosure Study
notation.staveTitle: Framing Target Notes with Diatonic Above and Chromatic Below

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: Keep alternate picking relaxed. Do not accent the approach notes—accent the target note when it lands on beat 1 for maximum harmonic punch.

exercises.title: Double Chromatic Run to the 5th
exercises.description: Targeting the 5th yields consonant, confident stability. In this exercise over C - F - G - C, two chromatic passing tones lead directly into the 5th of each chord on the downbeat, providing a classic swing and country-blues momentum.

patternNote.text: Formula: Two half-steps below ➔ Strong landing on the 5th of the arriving chord

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: Listen to the swagger of the chromatic passing tones. Because they are on weak beats, they do not clash with the harmony—they propel the listener toward the chord tone.

exercises.title: Rhythmic Anticipation: The '&' of 4 Push
exercises.description: Hitting your target note precisely on beat 1 is great for clarity, but master improvisers often anticipate the chord change by landing on the target note an eighth note early on the '&' of 4. This creates a syncopated 'push' that makes your lines feel modern and energetic.

patternNote.text: Anticipation Rule: Strike the upcoming chord's target note on beat 4-and, holding it through beat 1

notation.title: Syncopated Anticipation Target Study
notation.staveTitle: Anticipating Chord Tones on the '&' of Beat 4

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: Lock in with the hi-hat. Anticipating a chord tone pulls the groove forward; practice tapping your foot on quarters while your pick hits the syncopated off-beat.

exercises.title: The Master Study: Connecting Targets Across a Progression
exercises.description: This culminating 4-measure etude synthesizes all targeting principles: guide tone voice leading, chromatic approach notes, and enclosures over Dm7 - G7 - Cmaj7 - Am7. Play through fluidly, feeling how every single note serves as either an arrival point or a springboard to the next chord.

patternNote.text: Complete Synthesis: Guide tone voice leading + chromatic approaches + enclosures

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: Record your rhythm chords into a looper pedal and solo this etude over them. Listen for how the chromatic embellishments dissolve into pure harmonic resolution.

items.title: 3 Mistakes That Kill Target Note Soloing
items: Landing Non-Chord Tones on Beat 1: Striking a dissonant 4th or 9th without resolution on the downbeat makes your line sound clumsy rather than harmonically intentional.
Ignoring the 3rd: Over-relying on the root chord tone strips your phrases of emotional color. Target the 3rd to immediately reflect major or minor chord identity.
Unprepared Leaps: Jumping to a target note from wide, disconnected intervals without stepwise or chromatic preparation jars the listener's ear.

items.title: Masters of Target Note Improvisation
items: Charlie Parker: The pioneer of modern targeting; used chromatic approach notes and enclosures to navigate complex bebop cadences with supersonic precision.
Joe Pass: The consummate master of voice leading, outlining dense jazz chord progressions on solo guitar purely through 3rds, 7ths, and target resolutions.
Grant Green: Soulful hard-bop giant who blended blues inflections with laser-accurate guide tone landings on beats 1 and 3.
Larry Carlton: Steely Dan session legend renowned for hitting the sweet 3rd of every changing chord with glorious vocal sustain and tasteful slides.

items.title: The 15-Minute Daily Target Note Workout
items: Block 1: Downbeat 3rd Targeting (5 min) - Pick any 2-chord vamp. Improvise freely using scales, but you MUST hit the 3rd of each chord squarely on beat 1.
Block 2: Half-Step Approaches (5 min) - Lead into each target note by playing one fret below on the eighth note immediately preceding the chord change.
Block 3: Bebop Enclosure Practice (5 min) - Practice surrounding target chord tones with one diatonic scale step above and one chromatic step below before landing.
